H1: Gender will have an effect on the perception of constraints of leaving a relationship 

->IV: Gender (categorical): SEX
->DV:Perception of constraints of leaving relationship (conitnuous): relmob

H2: Daily use of social media and daily time spent enhancing appearance will have a positive correlation

V1: Daily use of socail media (continuous): Time_social_media_1
V2: Daily time spent enhancing appearance (continuous): sum of eight Time_A_ items


```{r setting up}
library(codebook)

#load the original dataset

###JK: Please match the capitalization of your folder names in your paths. ###
# Your repository contains a folder named Data, with a capital D.
# Lowercase data may work on your computer but fail on a computer that distinguishes uppercase and lowercase paths.
# Replace the read.csv() line below with:
# raw <- read.csv("Data/raw/data_doctored.csv")
###  End of comment ###

raw <- read.csv("data/raw/data_doctored.csv")

#Check dimensions and variable names 
dim(raw)
names(raw)
str(raw)
```
```{r}

###JK: I recommend keeping ResponseId in both hypothesis datasets so you can trace each row back to the original response. ###
# Your current calculations do not require the ID, but keeping it makes it easier to investigate unusual values and check for duplicates.
# Add the following line as the first entry inside each of the two data.frame() calls below, keeping the comma:
#   ResponseId = raw$ResponseId,
# After creating the datasets, you can check the IDs with:
# sum(is.na(h1Data$ResponseId))
# sum(duplicated(h1Data$ResponseId))
# sum(is.na(h2Data$ResponseId))
# sum(duplicated(h2Data$ResponseId))
###  End of comment ###

# H1: Gender and relationship constraints
h1Data <- data.frame(
  Sex = raw$Sex,
  relmob = raw$relmob
)

# H2: Social media use and appearance time
h2Data <- data.frame(
  Time_social_media = raw$Time_social_media_1,
  Time_A_makeup = raw$Time_A_makeup_1,
  Time_A_hyg = raw$Time_A_hyg_1,
  Time_A_cosm = raw$Time_A_cosm_1,
  Time_A_exercise = raw$Time_A_exercise_1,
  Time_A_hair = raw$Time_A_hair_1,
  Time_A_dress = raw$Time_A_dress_1,
  Time_A_diet = raw$Time_A_diet_1,
  Time_A_other = raw$Time_A_other_1
)

# Calculate total appearance-enhancement time
appearance_items <- c(
  "Time_A_makeup", "Time_A_hyg", "Time_A_cosm",
  "Time_A_exercise", "Time_A_hair", "Time_A_dress",
  "Time_A_diet", "Time_A_other"
)

h2Data$Appearance_time <- rowSums(
  h2Data[, appearance_items],
  na.rm = FALSE
)

###JK: Convert Sex to a factor because your H1 treats gender as categories, not a numerical score. ###
# The values 0, 1, 2, and 3 identify different response categories; they do not represent increasing amounts of gender.
# var_label() adds a description but does not change the variable's type.
# Add this code here, before assigning labels and creating h1Data_complete:
# h1Data$Sex <- factor(
#   h1Data$Sex,
#   levels = c(0, 1, 2, 3),
#   labels = c("Men", "Women", "Non-binary", "Prefer not to say")
# )
# table(h1Data$Sex, useNA = "ifany")
# str(h1Data$Sex)
###  End of comment ###

###JK: Please use Section 8, "Add labels and generate codebooks," in my Lab03 example script as a guide for expanding these descriptions. ###
# Your labels name the variables, but readers also need to know the category codes, response ranges, units, and what higher values mean.
# For Appearance_time, also explain which items are added and that all eight responses are required to calculate the total.
# Follow the var_label() examples in that section, using the information for your own variables from the codebook.
###  End of comment ###

# Add descriptive labels
var_label(h1Data$Sex) <- "Gender"
var_label(h1Data$relmob) <- "Perceived constraints on leaving a relationship"

var_label(h2Data$Time_social_media) <- "Daily time spent using social media"
var_label(h2Data$Appearance_time) <- "Total daily time spent enhancing appearance"
# Check the datasets
head(h1Data)
head(h2Data)
```
```{r}
#check variables 
table(raw$Sex, useNA = "ifany")
summary(raw$relmob)
summary(raw$Time_social_media_1)
summary(h2Data$Appearance_time)
```
```{r}
# Count answered appearance-time items per person
h2Data$Appearance_items_answered <- rowSums(
  !is.na(h2Data[, appearance_items])
)

table(h2Data$Appearance_items_answered)
```
```{r}
sum(
  !is.na(h2Data$Time_social_media) &
  !is.na(h2Data$Appearance_time)
)
```
```{r}
# Keep complete cases for the H1 and H2 hypothesis datasets
h1Data_complete <- h1Data[
  complete.cases(h1Data), ]

h2Data_complete <- h2Data[
  complete.cases(h2Data[, c(
    "Time_social_media", "Appearance_time"
  )]), ]

###JK: Please inspect unusually large totals. ###
# In the current data, 552 participants' appearance-time totals exceed 1,440 minutes (24 hours).
# The maximum total is 2,880 minutes, so these totals need attention before interpreting them as actual time spent in a day.
# Inspect them and explain how you will interpret or handle them.
# You can check them with:
# summary(h2Data_complete$Appearance_time)
# sum(h2Data_complete$Appearance_time > 1440)
# head(h2Data_complete[h2Data_complete$Appearance_time > 1440,
#                      c(appearance_items, "Appearance_time")])
# Please include the minutes unit and the all-eight-items requirement in the description of Appearance_time.
###  End of comment ###

# Check the number of complete cases
nrow(h1Data_complete)
nrow(h2Data_complete)
```
```{r save the data}

###JK: Save the complete-case datasets you just created, rather than the original unfiltered datasets. ###
# h1Data_complete and h2Data_complete contain 86,464 and 7,745 rows, respectively, with your current inclusion rules.
# The lines below save h1Data and h2Data instead, so the submitted CSV files each still contain all 117,294 rows, including missing values.

```

```{r}
#create codebook

###JK: Generate the codebooks from the same final datasets you save. ###
```
